topic: Quality Site Requirements, privacy and security

notes.front: What are the Quality Site Requirements (QSR)?
notes.back: The site standards that make volunteer return preparation accurate and site operation consistent.
notes.explanation: Partners must pass them on to every volunteer, and all partners and volunteers must follow all of them.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Purpose”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: The purpose of the Quality Site Requirements (QSR) is to ensure the quality and accuracy of tax return preparation and consistent site operation. Partners must communicate the QSR to all volunteers. All partners and volunteers must follow all QSR to ensure accurate tax return preparation and consistent site operation.
notes.example: Like the hygiene rules every branch of a restaurant chain follows, but for the way a free tax site prepares returns and runs itself.

notes.front: What is a Volunteer Tax Alert (VTA)?
notes.back: A tax law reference for volunteer sites; reviewers use it with Publications 4012 and 17 to check tax law determinations.
notes.explanation: Publication 5166 lists Volunteer Tax Alerts among the tax law references a quality reviewer consults to verify the accuracy of tax law decisions.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Quality Review Process”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: Review tax law references (Publication 4012 and Publication 17, Your Federal Income Tax (For Individuals), and Volunteer Tax Alerts), to verify the accuracy of tax law determinations.
notes.example: Like a safety bulletin sent to every garage about a car model, but telling volunteer sites about a tax law point.

notes.front: What is stockpiling of tax returns?
notes.back: Waiting more than three calendar days to submit a return once the site has all the necessary tax documents.
notes.explanation: Publication 5166 deals with it under QSR #6, Timely Filing of Tax Returns.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #6: Timely Filing of Tax Returns”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: Stockpiling is waiting more than three calendar days to submit the return once the site has all necessary tax documents.
notes.example: Like a post room that holds finished letters for a week to send them in one batch, but with completed tax returns.

notes.front: What is a site identification number (SIDN)?
notes.back: The number, the letter S followed by eight digits, that identifies the volunteer site on each return it prepares.
notes.explanation: It lets the Internal Revenue Service readily identify returns as volunteer-prepared.
notes.source: Publication 4491 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Training Guide, “Course Introduction: How does the IRS identify volunteer-prepared returns?”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: How does the IRS identify volunteer-prepared returns? Each return should be identified with the appropriate site identification number (SIDN) to ensure it is readily identifiable by the IRS. Your site’s SIDN is an 8-digit number preceded by the letter “S”
notes.example: Like a branch code printed on every receipt a chain store issues, but identifying the volunteer site on a tax return.

notes.front: What is an electronic filing identification number (EFIN)?
notes.back: The e-file number a partner applies for online through e-Services; every return a volunteer site prepares must carry the correct one.
notes.explanation: Getting it right is QSR #9, and each physical location needs its own.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #9: Correct Electronic Filing Identification Number (EFIN)”, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: All tax returns prepared by VITA/TCE sites must include the correct electronic filing identification number (EFIN). All partners must use the online IRS e-file application process found in E-Services on IRS.gov to apply for an EFIN or update an application. A separate EFIN is required for each physical location.
notes.example: Like a trader’s licence number that must appear on every invoice, but for sending returns electronically.

notes.front: What is personally identifiable information (PII), in Publication 4299?
notes.back: Details taxpayers give volunteers, such as names, addresses, Social Security numbers, birth dates and bank account information.
notes.explanation: Publication 4299 calls it a prime target for identity theft, so partners and volunteers must keep it confidential.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Background”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: Taxpayers using volunteer program services provide Personally Identifiable Information (PII) to the volunteers, such as names, addresses, Social Security Numbers (SSN), birth dates, and bank account information. This type of information is a prime target for identity theft. Therefore, partners and volunteers must keep the information confidential and protect it from unauthorized individuals and misuse.
notes.example: Like the details on a passport’s photo page, but also covering bank account and Social Security numbers.

notes.front: What is a volunteer site’s security plan?
notes.back: An annual plan, on Form 15272 or a similar document, of how the site safeguards taxpayer data.
notes.explanation: Every site must prepare one except Facilitated Self Assistance remote sites.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “VITA/TCE Security Plan”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: All VITA/TCE sites, except Facilitated Self Assistance (FSA) remote sites, must prepare an annual security plan to safeguard taxpayer data. Sites can use Form 15272, VITA/TCE Security Plan or a similar document which captures the same information to meet this requirement.
notes.example: Like a shop’s written routine for locking the till and the stockroom, but for tax papers, computers and software.

notes.front: Publication 4961 gives a brief description of each of the {{c1::ten}} Quality Site Requirements.
notes.back: ten
notes.explanation: For a full explanation of each one it sends the reader to Publication 5166.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #1 – Follow all Quality Site Requirements”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Refer to Publication 5166, VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, for a full explanation of each QSR. See a brief description of the ten QSR below

notes.front: What does QSR #1 cover?
notes.back: Certification.
notes.explanation: It requires volunteers to certify through the electronic tests on Link & Learn Taxes.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #1”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: QSR #1: Certification Volunteers must complete their certifications using the IRS electronic tests through Link & Learn Taxes (LLT).

notes.front: What does QSR #2 cover?
notes.back: The intake/interview and quality review process.
notes.explanation: Its aim is that every taxpayer can be confident of accurate return preparation and quality service.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #2”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: QSR #2: Intake/Interview and Quality Review Process All taxpayers using the services offered through the Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA) and Tax Counseling for the Elderly (TCE) programs should be confident they are receiving accurate return preparation and quality service.

notes.front: What does QSR #3 cover?
notes.back: Confirming photo identification and taxpayer identification numbers.
notes.explanation: The coordinator must have a process for checking who the taxpayers are and what their numbers are.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #3”, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: QSR #3: Confirming Photo Identification and Taxpayer Identification Numbers (TIN) Coordinators must have a process in place to confirm taxpayers’ identities and taxpayer identification numbers (TIN).

notes.front: What does QSR #4 cover?
notes.back: Reference materials.
notes.explanation: It lists the materials every site must have on hand, on paper or electronically.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #4”, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: QSR #4: Reference Materials All sites must have, in paper or electronic form, the following reference materials available for use by IRS tax law certified volunteers:

notes.front: What does QSR #5 cover?
notes.back: The volunteer agreement (Form 13615).
notes.explanation: Every volunteer, whatever the role, signs the agreement each year.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #5”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: QSR #5: Volunteer Agreement Form 13615, Volunteer Standards of Conduct Agreement – VITA/TCE Programs Annually, all volunteers (coordinators, return preparers, quality reviewers, greeters, screeners, client facilitators, etc.) must complete the Volunteer Standards of Conduct (VSC) certification.

notes.front: What does QSR #6 cover?
notes.back: Timely filing of tax returns.
notes.explanation: The site needs a process so that every return is e-filed or handed to the taxpayer in time.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #6”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: QSR #6: Timely Filing of Tax Returns All sites must have a process in place to ensure every tax return is timely electronically filed or delivered to the taxpayer.

notes.front: What does QSR #7 cover?
notes.back: Civil rights.
notes.explanation: Everyone who seeks help must be able to get information on Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #7”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: QSR #7: Civil Rights All VITA/TCE sites must make available to all taxpayers who seek services at the site information on Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964

notes.front: What does QSR #8 cover?
notes.back: The correct site identification number (SIDN).
notes.explanation: Every return the site prepares must carry its own correct site number.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #8”, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: QSR #8: Correct Site Identification Number (SIDN) All tax returns prepared by VITA/TCE sites must include the correct site identification number (SIDN).

notes.front: What does QSR #9 cover?
notes.back: The correct electronic filing identification number (EFIN).
notes.explanation: Every return the site prepares must carry the correct e-file number.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #9”, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: QSR #9: Correct Electronic Filing Identification Number (EFIN) All tax returns prepared by VITA/TCE sites must include the correct electronic filing identification number (EFIN).

notes.front: What does QSR #10 cover?
notes.back: Security, privacy and confidentiality.
notes.explanation: Publication 4299 is its resource document for protecting personal information.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #10”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: QSR #10: Security, Privacy, and Confidentiality Publication 4299, Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, is the resource document for guidance on securing and protecting personally identifiable information (PII)

notes.front: When does a volunteer’s failure to meet a QSR breach the Volunteer Standards of Conduct?
notes.back: When the volunteer refuses to adhere to, comply with or follow the QSR.
notes.explanation: That refusal breaks the first standard of conduct, “Follow all Quality Site Requirements”.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Violation of Volunteer Standards of Conduct #1”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: If any volunteer refuses to adhere to, comply with, or follow a QSR they have violated Volunteer Standards of Conduct (VSC) #1, Follow all Quality Site Requirements.

notes.front: A site reviewer finds no civil rights poster on display. The coordinator puts one up straight away. Has anyone breached the Volunteer Standards of Conduct?
notes.back: A: no, because the problem was corrected.
notes.explanation: Publication 4961 says not meeting a QSR becomes a breach only when volunteers refuse to follow it.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “VSC #1 – Follow all Quality Site Requirements”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Non-adherence to any QSR only becomes a violation of the VSC if volunteers refuse to follow the QSR. If the problem is corrected, it is not a violation of the VSC.
notes.choices:
A) No, because the problem was corrected
B) Yes, the coordinator breached the first standard
C) Yes, every volunteer at the site breached it
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong: a QSR problem that is put right is not a breach; only a refusal to follow the QSR would be.

notes.front: How does a site review score a site’s adherence to the QSR?
notes.back: 10 percentage points for each QSR rated “Met”, out of a possible 100.
notes.explanation: The review sheets mark the measured questions for each QSR in bold, and the points add up to an adherence rate.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Site Review Forms and Measures”, PDF p. 3
notes.evidence: Form 6729 and Form 6729-D have measured questions shown in bold text that measure site adherence to each QSR. Each site will receive 10 percentage points for each QSR rated as “Met” for a total of 100 potential points or an adherence rate of 100 percent.

notes.front: Under QSR #1, how must a volunteer who prefers to take a certification test on paper finish it?
notes.back: By transcribing the Form 6744 answers into the test on Link & Learn Taxes.
notes.explanation: Paper is allowed for taking the test, but the answers still have to end up in Link & Learn Taxes.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #1: Certification”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: Volunteers who prefer to take the Certification Test on paper utilizing Form 6744, VITA/TCE Volunteer Assistor’s Test or Retest, may continue to complete the test using that method but must transcribe their answers to the Test in LLT.

notes.front: Mid-morning, a reviewer finds that one preparer has not yet passed the certifications her role needs. She is halfway through a return. What happens?
notes.back: A: she finishes that return, a certified volunteer quality reviews it, and she prepares no more until certified.
notes.explanation: Publication 5166 lets the current return be completed but bars any others until the volunteer certifies.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Examples of not meeting QSR #1”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: Volunteers should complete the tax return they are currently preparing. The volunteers may not prepare any other tax returns until they become certified. Another IRS tax law certified volunteer preparer must quality review the tax return for accuracy.
notes.choices:
A) She finishes it, a certified volunteer reviews it, and she prepares no more until certified
B) She stops at once and the return is destroyed
C) She carries on for the day and certifies that evening
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the current return may be completed. C is wrong: she may not prepare any other return until she is certified.

notes.front: A reviewer finds that none of the volunteers at a site has certified as required, and no certified preparers can come from other sites. What must happen?
notes.back: A: close the site for the day and refer the remaining taxpayers to other volunteer sites.
notes.explanation: Publication 5166’s alternative to closing may be to seek help from certified preparers at other sites.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Examples of not meeting QSR #1”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: Use care to inform the remaining taxpayers that the site must close for the day. An alternative to closing the site may be to seek help of IRS tax law certified volunteer preparers from other sites. If this is not possible, refer the remaining taxpayers to other VITA/TCE site locations
notes.choices:
A) Close for the day and refer the remaining taxpayers to other sites
B) Keep preparing returns but skip the quality review
C) Stay open while the volunteers take the tests between clients
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: uncertified volunteers cannot prepare returns at all. C is wrong: the site must close and cannot reopen until the volunteers certify.

notes.front: Under QSR #2, what must a site use for every return a certified volunteer prepares?
notes.back: Form 13614-C, the Intake/Interview and Quality Review Sheet, and a complete quality review process.
notes.explanation: Form 13614-C guides the preparer through the interview and gathers what an accurate return needs.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “QSR #2, Intake/Interview and Quality Review Process”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: All sites must use Form 13614-C, Intake/Interview and Quality Review Sheet, for every tax return prepared by an IRS-certified volunteer. Form 13614-C guides the IRS-certified volunteer preparer through the interview with the taxpayer and allows them to gather all necessary information to prepare an accurate return.

notes.front: When is a volunteer-prepared return considered accurate?
notes.back: When tax law is applied correctly and the return is free from error, based on Form 13614-C, the interview and the supporting documents.
notes.explanation: This is the standard the complete quality review process checks every return against.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “QSR #2, Intake/Interview and Quality Review Process”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: A tax return is considered accurate when tax law is applied correctly, and the completed return is free from error based on the completed Form 13614-C, Intake/Interview and Quality Review Sheet (or Form 13614-NR), the taxpayer's interview and the taxpayer’s supporting documentation.

notes.front: At a busy site, preparers key in returns straight from the taxpayers’ documents without talking the answers through with them. Which QSR is not being met?
notes.back: A: QSR #2.
notes.explanation: Publication 5166 gives “Not interviewing the taxpayer” as an example of not meeting QSR #2.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Examples of not meeting QSR #2”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: Examples of not meeting QSR #2: 1. Not using Form 13614-C. 2. Not interviewing the taxpayer.
notes.choices:
A) QSR #2
B) QSR #3
C) QSR #6
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: QSR #3 covers photo identification and taxpayer identification numbers. C is wrong: QSR #6 covers timely filing.

notes.front: A site prepares returns from documents taxpayers drop off, without any signed Form 14446. Which QSR is not being met?
notes.back: A: QSR #2.
notes.explanation: Not using Form 14446 at sites using virtual models is one of Publication 5166’s examples of not meeting QSR #2.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Examples of not meeting QSR #2”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: 3. Not using Form 14446 at sites using Virtual VITA/TCE models. 4. Does not quality review all returns.
notes.choices:
A) QSR #2
B) QSR #10
C) QSR #5
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: QSR #10 covers security, privacy and confidentiality. C is wrong: QSR #5 covers the volunteer agreement.

notes.front: A site lets preparers pick any return from the queue, whatever its certification level. Which QSR is not being met?
notes.back: A: QSR #2.
notes.explanation: QSR #2 needs a process that keeps returns in scope and assigns them to preparers and reviewers at their certification level.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Examples of not meeting QSR #2”, PDF p. 13
notes.evidence: 6. No process which ensures returns are within scope and volunteer preparers and quality reviewers are assigned returns at their certification level.
notes.choices:
A) QSR #2
B) QSR #1
C) QSR #4
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: QSR #1 covers certification. C is wrong: QSR #4 covers reference materials.

notes.front: In a virtual model, when must the taxpayer sign Form 14446?
notes.back: Before leaving any documents at the site; the spouse signs too if married filing jointly.
notes.explanation: The volunteer must first explain the virtual method and its steps during intake.
notes.source: Publication 5838 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Intake/Interview and Quality Review Handbook, “1-5: Additional Requirements for Virtual VITA/TCE Model”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: During the intake process, the volunteer must explain the virtual method(s) and step-bystep procedures to the taxpayer. Taxpayer (and spouse if married filing joint) must sign Form 14446 before leaving behind any documents at a VITA/TCE.

notes.front: If a site keeps a taxpayer’s Form 13614-C after the return is complete, how long may it keep it?
notes.back: Until the return has been accepted, and no later than 31 December of the return preparation year.
notes.explanation: The alternative is to give the form back to the taxpayer with their copy of the return.
notes.source: Publication 5838 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Intake/Interview and Quality Review Handbook, “1-6: Maintaining Form 13614-C”, PDF p. 7
notes.evidence: After the return is complete, the Form 13614-C can be returned to the taxpayer with their copy of the return, or the site/partner may retain the Form 13614-C until the return has been accepted but no later than December 31 of the return preparation year.

notes.front: Under QSR #3, when must volunteers confirm taxpayers’ identities and identification numbers?
notes.back: Before preparing the return, and again at quality review before the taxpayer signs and receives a copy.
notes.explanation: The quality reviewer repeats the verification procedures rather than relying on the preparer’s check.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #3: Confirming Photo Identification and Taxpayer Identification Numbers (TIN)”, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: All volunteers must perform the verification procedures prior to tax return preparation. In addition, the quality reviewer must perform the verification procedures again during quality review before taxpayer signs and receives a copy of the prepared tax return.

notes.front: Under QSR #3, whose original photo identification must volunteers review?
notes.back: The taxpayer’s, and the spouse’s too if they are married filing jointly.
notes.explanation: The spouse’s identification is needed only when the couple is married filing jointly.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #3: Confirming Photo Identification and Taxpayer Identification Numbers (TIN)”, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: Original photo identification (ID) for the taxpayer (and spouse, if married filing jointly); and

notes.front: Under QSR #3, for whom must volunteers confirm Social Security numbers or ITINs?
notes.back: For everyone listed on the return.
notes.explanation: That includes dependants, not only the people who sign.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #3: Confirming Photo Identification and Taxpayer Identification Numbers (TIN)”, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: Social Security numbers (SSN) and individual taxpayer identification numbers (ITIN) for everyone listed on the tax return and

notes.front: Besides photo identification and identification numbers, what does the QSR #3 process check for everyone on the return?
notes.back: The correct spelling of their names.
notes.explanation: Publication 5166 lists name spelling as the third thing the verification process must review.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #3: Confirming Photo Identification and Taxpayer Identification Numbers (TIN)”, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: Correct spelling of names for everyone listed on the tax return

notes.front: What are two kinds of original photo identification Publication 4299 lets a preparer review for a taxpayer?
notes.back: Any two, among others: a U.S. driver’s licence; employer, school, state, military or national identification; a visa; a passport.
notes.explanation: Volunteers must use judgement when accepting any other valid form of identification.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Validating Taxpayer(s) Identity and Identification Number(s)”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: The volunteer must review an original photo identification (ID) such as valid driver’s license (U.S.), employer ID, school ID, state ID (U.S.), Military ID, national ID, visa, or passport. Volunteers must use judgment when accepting any other valid form of identification.

notes.front: When may a site make an exception to requiring original photo identification from a taxpayer?
notes.back: Only in extreme circumstances, and only with the site coordinator’s approval.
notes.explanation: Otherwise a taxpayer who cannot prove identity must be told to come back with acceptable identification.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Validating Taxpayer(s) Identity and Identification Number(s)”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: If a taxpayer cannot substantiate his/her identity, or if the volunteer is uncomfortable accepting the items presented as proof of identity, the taxpayer must be advised to return with an acceptable form of identification. Exceptions to requiring an original photo ID must only be made under extreme circumstances and require site coordinator approval.

notes.front: A preparer is uneasy about the only identification a new taxpayer offers: a library card with no photo. There are no extreme circumstances. What should the preparer do?
notes.back: A: advise the taxpayer to come back with an acceptable form of identification.
notes.explanation: Exceptions need extreme circumstances and the site coordinator’s approval; a preparer cannot grant one.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Validating Taxpayer(s) Identity and Identification Number(s)”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: If a taxpayer cannot substantiate his/her identity, or if the volunteer is uncomfortable accepting the items presented as proof of identity, the taxpayer must be advised to return with an acceptable form of identification.
notes.choices:
A) Advise the taxpayer to return with acceptable identification
B) Accept the card and note it on Form 13614-C
C) Prepare the return and check identity at quality review
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: a preparer cannot make an exception. C is wrong: identity must be confirmed before preparation, not only at review.

notes.front: What may a taxpayer provide to prove a Social Security number?
notes.back: The Social Security card, original or a paper or electronic copy, or an acceptable substitute issued by the Social Security Administration.
notes.explanation: Copies may be paper or electronic, not only originals.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Validating Taxpayer(s) Identity and Identification Number(s)”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: Taxpayers must provide original or copies (paper or electronic) of social security cards or an acceptable substitute such as Form SSA-1099 and/or any other verification issued from the SSA.

notes.front: What must the volunteer review for a taxpayer or dependant who does not qualify for a Social Security number?
notes.back: An ITIN card or letter issued by the Internal Revenue Service, or help them apply for an ITIN.
notes.explanation: This covers dependants as well as taxpayers.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Validating Taxpayer(s) Identity and Identification Number(s)”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: For taxpayers or dependents who do not qualify for an SSN, the volunteer must review an IRS-issued ITIN card or letter or assist with applying for an ITIN.

notes.front: According to Publication 4299, what is one of the top reasons electronic returns are delayed in processing?
notes.back: Names that do not match the Social Security number or ITIN records.
notes.explanation: It comes in Publication 4299’s section on validating identity and identification numbers.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Validating Taxpayer(s) Identity and Identification Number(s)”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: The mismatch of names and SSN or ITIN information is one of the top reasons for delays in processing electronic tax returns.

notes.front: A preparer takes a taxpayer’s word for her three children’s Social Security numbers, with no documents and no exception approved. Which QSR is not being met?
notes.back: A: QSR #3.
notes.explanation: Not confirming the numbers for everyone on the return with acceptable documents is an example of not meeting QSR #3.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Examples of not meeting QSR #3”, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: 3. Not confirming TIN for everyone listed on the tax return using acceptable documents. 4. Not securing coordinator approval for exceptions to these requirements as mandated in Publication 4299.
notes.choices:
A) QSR #3
B) QSR #2
C) QSR #10
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: QSR #2 covers intake, interview and quality review. C is wrong: QSR #10 covers security, privacy and confidentiality.

notes.front: Under QSR #4, which publication number is the required reference “Your Federal Income Tax (For Individuals)”?
notes.back: Publication 17.
notes.explanation: Every site must have it available to certified volunteers, on paper or electronically.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #4: Reference Materials”, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: All sites must have, in paper or electronic form, the following reference materials available for use by IRS tax law certified volunteers: • Publication 17, Your Federal Income Tax (For Individuals)

notes.front: Under QSR #4, which publication number is the required Volunteer Resource Guide?
notes.back: Publication 4012.
notes.explanation: Its flow charts and decision trees help volunteers decide filing status and credit eligibility.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #4: Reference Materials”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: Volunteers can make determinations following one of the flow charts or decision trees in Publication 4012.

notes.front: Under QSR #4, which required reference is “Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust”?
notes.back: Publication 4299.
notes.explanation: Coordinators must have access to it at the site during tax preparation hours, because security is a high priority.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #4: Reference Materials”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: SPEC views security as a high priority. To help with potential security concerns, coordinators must have access to the Publication 4299 at the site during tax preparation hours.

notes.front: Besides three publications, what alerts must every site have available under QSR #4?
notes.back: Volunteer Tax Alerts and Quality Site Requirement Alerts, or the CyberTax Alerts issued by Tax-Aide.
notes.explanation: They sit alongside Publications 17, 4012 and 4299 as required reference materials.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #4: Reference Materials”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: Volunteer Tax Alerts (VTA) and Quality Site Requirement Alerts (QSRA) or CyberTax Alerts issued by Tax-Aide

notes.front: Why does QSR #4 stress reference materials, according to Publication 5166?
notes.back: Many preparation errors happen when deciding filing status and eligibility for tax credits, and the references help minimise errors.
notes.explanation: Publication 4012’s flow charts and decision trees are meant for exactly those decisions.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #4: Reference Materials”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: For example, many errors in tax return preparation occur during the determination of filing status and eligibility for tax credits. Volunteers can make determinations following one of the flow charts or decision trees in Publication 4012. The availability of key tax law reference materials supports the use of these resources and minimizes return errors.

notes.front: Within what time must coordinators review and discuss each Volunteer Tax Alert with their volunteers?
notes.back: Within seven business days after it is issued.
notes.explanation: The alerts are emailed to volunteers listed as site coordinators and posted on the Site Coordinator Corner.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #4: Reference Materials”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: Coordinators must review and discuss with their volunteers all VTA and QSRA or CyberTax Alerts, within seven business days after IRS issuance. VTA and QSRA are emailed out systemically to volunteers listed as site coordinators. The alerts are also available on the Site Coordinator Corner on IRS.gov.

notes.front: A coordinator receives a new VTA by email and plans to mention it at the end-of-season meeting in six weeks. Is that enough?
notes.back: A: no; it must be reviewed and discussed with volunteers within seven business days of issue.
notes.explanation: Having no process to make sure all volunteers review every alert is an example of not meeting QSR #4.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Examples of not meeting QSR #4”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: The site does not have a process to ensure all volunteers review all VTA and QSRA or CyberTax Alerts. The reviewer must explain to the coordinator the requirement to review and discuss with volunteers all VTA and QSRA or CyberTax Alerts within seven business days after IRS issuance.
notes.choices:
A) No, within seven business days of issue
B) Yes, any time before the season ends
C) Yes, if the alert is pinned on the notice board
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the limit is seven business days, not the end of the season. C is wrong: the coordinator must review and discuss the alert with volunteers, not just post it.

notes.front: Under QSR #5, what must every volunteer do each year?
notes.back: Pass the Volunteer Standards of Conduct certification and agree to the standards by signing and dating Form 13615.
notes.explanation: This applies to every role: coordinators, preparers, reviewers, greeters, screeners and client facilitators.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #5: Volunteer Agreement”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: Annually, all volunteers (coordinators, return preparers, quality reviewers, greeters, screeners, client facilitators, etc.) must complete the Volunteer Standards of Conduct (VSC) certification. In addition they must agree to follow the VSC by signing and dating Form 13615.

notes.front: Who are two people a partner may appoint as the approving official who certifies Form 13615?
notes.back: Any two of: the coordinator, a sponsoring partner official, an instructor, an Internal Revenue Service contact.
notes.explanation: The partner makes the appointment.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #5: Volunteer Agreement”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: This approving official can be the coordinator, sponsoring partner official, instructor, or IRS contact, as appointed by the partner.

notes.front: What are two kinds of government-issued photo identification an approving official may accept from a volunteer?
notes.back: Any two of: a valid U.S. driver’s licence, a U.S. state identification, military or national identification, a visa, Global Entry identification, a passport.
notes.explanation: Partners and coordinators may review this identification electronically.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #5: Volunteer Agreement”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: SPEC partners and coordinators can review volunteers’ government-issued photo ID electronically. Government-issued photo identification (ID) includes valid driver’s license (U.S.), state ID (U.S.), Military ID, national ID, visa, Global Entry ID, or passport.

notes.front: Two certified preparers are working, but the coordinator has not yet received their signed Forms 13615. What may they do?
notes.back: A: finish the return each is working on, then prepare or review no others until the signed forms arrive.
notes.explanation: Publication 5166 gives this as an example of not meeting QSR #5 and allows only the current returns to be completed.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Examples of not meeting QSR #5”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: Volunteers are certified but the partner or coordinator has not received signed Forms 13615. The IRS tax law certified volunteer preparer or quality reviewer may complete the tax return they are currently preparing or reviewing. The volunteers may not prepare or quality review any other tax returns until the partner or coordinator receives the volunteers’ signed Forms 13615.
notes.choices:
A) Finish the current return, then stop until the signed forms arrive
B) Carry on for the rest of the day
C) Stop at once and abandon the current returns
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: no other returns may be prepared or reviewed until the forms arrive. C is wrong: the return in progress may be completed.

notes.front: A new volunteer starts screening taxpayers before anyone has signed and dated her Form 13615. Which QSR is not being met?
notes.back: A: QSR #5.
notes.explanation: The volunteer and the approving official must both sign and date Form 13615 before the volunteer works at the site.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Examples of not meeting QSR #5”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: The volunteer or the partner’s approving official did not sign and date Form 13615 prior to the volunteer working at the site.
notes.choices:
A) QSR #5
B) QSR #1
C) QSR #3
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: QSR #1 covers certification. C is wrong: QSR #3 covers photo identification and taxpayer identification numbers.

notes.front: When does a site’s three calendar days to e-file a return begin?
notes.back: Once the taxpayer has finished intake and interview, given all documents, completed quality review and signed Form 8879.
notes.explanation: From then the site has three calendar days to e-file; waiting longer is stockpiling.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “E-filing Returns and Stockpiling of Returns”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: This means the taxpayer has completed the intake/interview process, provided all necessary tax documents, completed the quality review and has provided consent to the site to e-file the return by signing of Form 8879, IRS e-file Signature Authorization. Once these steps have been completed, the VITA/TCE site has three calendar days to e-file the return.

notes.front: A taxpayer signs Form 8879 on Monday after a completed quality review. The site plans to transmit all its returns together the following Monday. What is the problem?
notes.back: A: that is stockpiling; the return must be e-filed within three calendar days.
notes.explanation: The three days run from when the site has everything, which here is Monday.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “E-filing Returns and Stockpiling of Returns”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: Tax returns must be e-filed no more than three calendar days after the site has secured all necessary information from the taxpayer and completed all necessary tax preparation steps required to file the taxpayers return electronically.
notes.choices:
A) It is stockpiling; e-file within three calendar days
B) No problem, because a week is a reasonable time
C) No problem, as long as the taxpayer agrees
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the limit is three calendar days, not a week. C is wrong: the rule is set by Publication 5166, not by the taxpayer’s agreement.

notes.front: A site finishes a return, fully signed, in early January, days before the Internal Revenue Service opens e-file for the season. Is holding it stockpiling?
notes.back: A: no; the three days start only when e-file opens, and the taxpayer must be told it cannot be sent until then.
notes.explanation: Publication 5166 excludes the period before e-file opens from the three-calendar-day rule.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Exception to General Rule – Returns Completed Prior to IRS E-File System Opening”, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: The three calendar days rule would start from the time the IRS officially starts accepting e-filed returns. Sites completing returns for taxpayers prior to the start of IRS E-filing system being available to electronically file returns, must tell taxpayers that it cannot transmit returns to the IRS until the date the IRS accepts transmission of electronic returns.
notes.choices:
A) No, the three days start when e-file opens; tell the taxpayer
B) Yes, it must be printed and mailed instead
C) Yes, unless it is sent within three days of signing
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong: the three-day rule does not run before the Internal Revenue Service officially opens e-file.

notes.front: A return cannot be finished because the taxpayer stops responding. What must the site tell the taxpayer?
notes.back: That the return has been deactivated in the software, and to come back to collect their tax documents.
notes.explanation: The same applies to delays from rejects, an unsigned Form 8879 or volunteer staffing.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “E-filing Returns and Stockpiling of Returns”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: If due to lack of response, delays with resolving rejects, signing Form 8879 or volunteer staffing, sites must notify taxpayers that the return has been deactivated in the tax preparation software and to return to the site to pick up their tax documents.

notes.front: Before a site e-files Form 4868 for a taxpayer, what must the taxpayer sign?
notes.back: Form 8878, the e-file signature authorisation for Form 4868.
notes.explanation: The same authorisation form also covers Form 2350.
notes.source: Publication 4961 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Standards of Conduct – Ethics Training, “QSR #6, Extension to File Returns”, PDF p. 10
notes.evidence: In order to e-file the Form 4868 on behalf of the taxpayer, the Form 8878, IRS E-file Signature Authorization for the Form 4868 or Form 2350 MUST be signed by the taxpayer prior to the e-filing of the Form 4868.

notes.front: A coordinator has no process for e-filing returns within three calendar days or for retrieving acknowledgements. Which QSR is not being met?
notes.back: A: QSR #6.
notes.explanation: Both gaps are among Publication 5166’s examples of not meeting QSR #6.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Examples of not meeting QSR #6”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: E-filing the taxpayer’s return within three calendar days from the date all necessary information has been received and all tax preparation steps have been completed.
notes.choices:
A) QSR #6
B) QSR #2
C) QSR #9
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: QSR #2 covers intake, interview and quality review. C is wrong: QSR #9 covers the electronic filing identification number.

notes.front: Which poster do volunteer sites provide to meet QSR #7?
notes.back: The current Publication 4053, “Your Civil Rights are Protected”, in English and Spanish; Tax-Aide sites may use their own current poster.
notes.explanation: The poster is how the site makes information on Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 available to everyone who seeks services.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #7: Civil Rights”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 by providing the current Publication 4053 (en-sp), Your Civil Rights are Protected Poster for IRS Assisted Programs (VITA/TCE/LITC) (English & Spanish), or a current D143, AARP Foundation Tax-Aide (poster).

notes.front: Where must the civil rights poster be at a traditional site, and what do virtual sites do?
notes.back: Visible at the first point of contact between taxpayer and volunteer; virtual sites send it or make it available to everyone.
notes.explanation: The rule differs by type of site: displayed in person, sent or made available virtually.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #7: Civil Rights”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: At a traditional site, the poster must be visible at the first point of contact between the taxpayer and volunteer. For virtual sites, the poster must be sent or made available to all seeking services.

notes.front: A taxpayer’s return is out of scope, so the site cannot prepare it. What does QSR #7 still require for this taxpayer?
notes.back: A: access to the civil rights information; Publication 4454 can be offered.
notes.explanation: Taxpayers must have access to it even without a return prepared, and Publication 4454 is meant for when the site cannot provide service.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #7: Civil Rights”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: when the site cannot provide tax preparation services (for example, lack of information to prepare the return, the return is not within scope of the VITA/ TCE program). Taxpayers must have access to the civil rights information even if they do not have a tax return prepared.
notes.choices:
A) Access to the civil rights information, for example Publication 4454
B) Nothing, because no return is prepared
C) Only the tax records envelope, Publication 730
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the information must be available even when no return is prepared. C is wrong: Publication 730 is not an acceptable civil rights notice.

notes.front: Why can a site not rely on Publication 730, the tax records envelope, to tell taxpayers their civil rights?
notes.back: It reaches only taxpayers who receive service, not those who are denied it.
notes.explanation: The civil rights information must reach everyone who seeks services, including people who are turned away.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #7: Civil Rights”, PDF p. 20
notes.evidence: It is not acceptable to use Publication 730 (en-sp) or the Tax-Aide envelope as the source for notifying the taxpayers of their civil rights. This product offers information to the taxpayer who receives service, not the taxpayer who is denied service.

notes.front: Under QSR #8, who must set the software so the correct SIDN appears on every return?
notes.back: The site’s e-file administrators, by setting the tax software defaults.
notes.explanation: Partners or coordinators should also work with the local territory office to confirm the correct number.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #8: Correct Site Identification Number (SIDN)”, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: E-file administrators must set tax software defaults to make sure the correct SIDN automatically appears on each tax return. Partners or coordinators should work with their local SPEC territory office to make sure they are using the correct SIDN.

notes.front: In which section of a return does the site’s SIDN appear?
notes.back: The Paid Preparer Use Only section, on every return the site prepares, paper or electronic.
notes.explanation: The coordinator provides the number, along with other guidelines for completing the return.
notes.source: Publication 4491 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Training Guide, “Course Introduction: How does the IRS identify volunteer-prepared returns?”, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: the Paid Preparer Use Only section on all returns you prepare, both paper and electronic. Your coordinator provides this number along with other necessary guidelines for completing the return.

notes.front: A reviewer finds the wrong SIDN on returns because a volunteer who also helps at another site is signed into that site’s account. What is the fix?
notes.back: A: the volunteer signs out and back in with the login for the site where they are preparing returns.
notes.explanation: Publication 5166 gives this cause and this resolution for an incorrect SIDN under QSR #8.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Examples of not meeting QSR #8”, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: The SIDN is incorrect on the return because the volunteer is signed into the wrong account. The resolution is the volunteer signs out and back in to the software using their login for the site where they are preparing returns.
notes.choices:
A) Sign out and back in with the login for this site
B) Apply for a new EFIN
C) Leave it, since the SIDN is only for statistics
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the problem is the account, not the EFIN. C is wrong: every return must carry the correct SIDN.

notes.front: A partner runs volunteer sites in two different buildings. How many EFINs does it need?
notes.back: Two: a separate EFIN is required for each physical location.
notes.explanation: Publication 5166 ties the EFIN to the physical location, not to the partner.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #9: Correct Electronic Filing Identification Number (EFIN)”, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: A separate EFIN is required for each physical location.

notes.front: A site runs a one-day ad hoc site at a community centre. Which numbers do volunteers use there?
notes.back: A: a second account with a different SIDN, but the main site’s EFIN.
notes.explanation: Publication 5166 sets up a second account for the ad hoc location while the EFIN stays the main site’s.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #9: Correct Electronic Filing Identification Number (EFIN)”, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: If the site is an ad hoc site, then a second Electronic Return Originator (ERO) account with a different SIDN is set up for volunteers to use at that location, but the site continues to use the EFIN of the main site.
notes.choices:
A) A different SIDN, but the main site’s EFIN
B) The main site’s SIDN and a new EFIN
C) A new SIDN and a new EFIN
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong: an ad hoc site keeps the main site’s EFIN and gets its own SIDN.

notes.front: Returns at a site carry the electronic filing number of a different partner’s office. Which QSR is not being met?
notes.back: A: QSR #9.
notes.explanation: Using an incorrect EFIN is Publication 5166’s example of not meeting QSR #9.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Example of not meeting QSR #9”, PDF p. 21
notes.evidence: Example of not meeting QSR #9: 1. The site is using an incorrect EFIN.
notes.choices:
A) QSR #9
B) QSR #8
C) QSR #5
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: QSR #8 covers the site identification number. C is wrong: QSR #5 covers the volunteer agreement.

notes.front: Under QSR #10, which publication must be available at every site, and in what form?
notes.back: Publication 4299, as a paper or electronic copy.
notes.explanation: It is the resource for securing and protecting PII shared by taxpayers, volunteers and partners.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #10: Security, Privacy, and Confidentiality”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: is the resource document for guidance on securing and protecting personally identifiable information (PII) shared by taxpayers, volunteers, and partners. A copy (paper or electronic) must be available at the site.

notes.front: Under QSR #10, what must protect every computer at the site?
notes.back: Passwords.
notes.explanation: Password protection is one of the security procedures every coordinator must have, as Publication 4299 describes.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #10: Security, Privacy, and Confidentiality”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: Protecting all computers with passwords.

notes.front: Under QSR #10, what kinds of internet connection may a site use?
notes.back: A hard-wired connection, or a wireless one that is encrypted and password protected.
notes.explanation: An open wireless network does not meet the security procedure.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #10: Security, Privacy, and Confidentiality”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: Using a hard-wired internet connection or encrypted and password protected wireless internet connection.

notes.front: Under QSR #10, on what basis are volunteers’ access privileges in the tax software limited?
notes.back: Their assigned roles.
notes.explanation: The same list also requires volunteer access to the software to be generally restricted.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #10: Security, Privacy, and Confidentiality”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: Limiting volunteer access privileges to the tax software based on assigned roles. • Generally restricting volunteer access to the tax software.

notes.front: Under QSR #10, when must a volunteer’s username in the tax software be deactivated?
notes.back: When the volunteer quits, resigns or no longer works at the site.
notes.explanation: It is the last of the security processes Publication 5166 lists under QSR #10.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #10: Security, Privacy, and Confidentiality”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: Deactivating usernames in the tax software when volunteers quit, resign, or are no longer working at the site.

notes.front: A volunteer who resigned in February can still sign in to the site’s tax software in March. Which QSR is not being met?
notes.back: A: QSR #10.
notes.explanation: Not deactivating usernames when volunteers leave is one of Publication 5166’s examples of not meeting QSR #10.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Examples of not meeting QSR #10”, PDF p. 23
notes.evidence: 8. Volunteer usernames are not deactivated in the tax software when volunteers quit, resign, or are no longer working at the site.
notes.choices:
A) QSR #10
B) QSR #5
C) QSR #1
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: QSR #5 covers the volunteer agreement. C is wrong: QSR #1 covers certification.

notes.front: By when must the site coordinator sign the security plan and submit it to the territory office?
notes.back: Before the site opens, and no later than 31 December.
notes.explanation: All partners must approve the plan as well.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #10: Security, Privacy, and Confidentiality”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: All partners must approve the security plan. The site coordinator must sign the form and submit the form to their SPEC territory office prior to opening of the site but no later than December 31.

notes.front: Who signs Form 15272 to approve a site’s security plan, and where is the approved plan kept?
notes.back: The relationship manager and the territory manager sign it; the territory office keeps it, not the site.
notes.explanation: The approved plan no longer has to be held at the site.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #10: Security, Privacy, and Confidentiality”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: The relationship manager and the territory manager must sign Form 15272 acknowledging approval of the security plan before the site opens. The territory office must maintain the approved security plans for each site. The approved security plan (Form 15272) is no longer required to be maintained at the site.

notes.front: A reviewer asks to see Publication 17 and the site has no copy, printed or electronic. Which QSR is not being met?
notes.back: A: QSR #4.
notes.explanation: Reference materials not being available in print or electronic form is Publication 5166’s first example of not meeting QSR #4.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “Examples of not meeting QSR #4”, PDF p. 15
notes.evidence: Reference materials are not available in print or electronic format for use by volunteers. The reviewer must promptly help the coordinator download the reference materials.
notes.choices:
A) QSR #4
B) QSR #1
C) QSR #10
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: QSR #1 covers certification. C is wrong: QSR #10 covers security, privacy and confidentiality.

notes.front: A site will open on 20 January. Its coordinator plans to sign and submit the security plan on 10 January. Does that meet the deadline?
notes.back: A: no; it must be submitted before the site opens and no later than 31 December.
notes.explanation: Both limits apply: before opening, and in any case by 31 December.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “QSR #10: Security, Privacy, and Confidentiality”, PDF p. 22
notes.evidence: The site coordinator must sign the form and submit the form to their SPEC territory office prior to opening of the site but no later than December 31.
notes.choices:
A) No, it was due by 31 December
B) Yes, because it is before the site opens
C) Yes, any time in the first week of opening
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: being before opening is not enough; the plan is also due by 31 December. C is wrong: the plan must be in before the site opens.

notes.front: When does information a taxpayer gives a volunteer become “return information” protected by section 6103 of the Internal Revenue Code?
notes.back: Only when the Internal Revenue Service receives, records or collects it.
notes.explanation: Even before then, volunteers face the criminal penalties of 18 U.S.C. 1905 for improper disclosure.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Background”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: Information provided by individual taxpayers to a VITA/TCE volunteer is not considered “return information” protected by IRC 6103 until the IRS receives, records or collects it. However, VITA/TCE volunteers are subject to the criminal penalty provisions of 18 USC 1905 for any improper disclosures of this information.

notes.front: What must partners and volunteers do about keeping records of taxpayers’ PII?
notes.back: Keep as little as possible, unless the taxpayer gives written consent to disclose and use it.
notes.explanation: Written consent to disclose and use is the stated exception.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Background”, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: Partners and volunteers must minimize the retention of any taxpayer PII records unless the taxpayer provides written consent to disclose and use as explained under Taxpayer Consents.

notes.front: A preparer needs to check a taxpayer’s bank account number at a crowded table. What should she do?
notes.back: A: point to the number on the screen or document and let the taxpayer confirm it, without reading it aloud.
notes.explanation: Publication 4299 says volunteers must not discuss PII out loud and suggests pointing to it instead.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Privacy During the Interview”, PDF p. 6
notes.evidence: During conversations with taxpayers, volunteers must not discuss PII information out loud. For example, volunteers can point to the computer screen or supporting document containing the PII information and the taxpayer could verify if the information is correct.
notes.choices:
A) Point to it and let the taxpayer confirm it silently
B) Read it out quietly
C) Ask a colleague at the next table to double-check it aloud
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong: PII must not be spoken aloud, and a colleague with no need to know should not see it.

notes.front: Over lunch, a volunteer tells two other volunteers how much a well-known local taxpayer earned. Is that acceptable?
notes.back: A: no; they have no need to know, since the return does not need their involvement.
notes.explanation: Publication 4299 allows sharing only with people whose involvement the return requires, even among volunteers.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Sharing the Information”, PDF p. 8
notes.evidence: It is not acceptable to share information with others, even another volunteer, if the tax return preparation does not require their involvement. For instance, sharing income information, birth dates, or even the marital status of taxpayers with other volunteers, taxpayers, family, or friends as a matter of curiosity or interest, is not acceptable.
notes.choices:
A) No, they have no need to know
B) Yes, because they are volunteers too
C) Yes, if no Social Security number is mentioned
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: being a volunteer does not create a need to know. C is wrong: even income, birth dates or marital status may not be shared out of curiosity.

notes.front: Returns are prepared with the taxpayer present. What are the three exceptions?
notes.back: A joint return with one spouse present; a minor child’s return with a parent or guardian present; an approved virtual model.
notes.explanation: Outside these three cases, the taxpayer must be present at the site.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Taxpayers Must Participate in Return Preparation”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: Volunteers must prepare all tax returns at the site with the taxpayer present unless (1) preparing a joint return for a married couple with one taxpayer present at the site or (2) preparing a return for a minor child in the presence of the child’s parent or guardian or (3) when using an approved Virtual VITA/TCE service model

notes.front: A man brings his adult sister’s documents and a note from her authorising him to act for her. She is not at the site, and it offers no virtual model. May the site prepare her return?
notes.back: A: no; the site must not prepare it without her participation.
notes.explanation: Publication 4299 rules this out even when the taxpayer has authorised someone else.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Taxpayers Must Participate in Return Preparation”, PDF p. 5
notes.evidence: Otherwise, VITA/TCE sites must not prepare a tax return without the taxpayer’s participation even if the taxpayer authorized another person to represent them for the preparation of a tax return.
notes.choices:
A) No, not without her participation
B) Yes, because she authorised him in writing
C) Yes, if he signs Form 8879 for her
notes.choicesExplained: B and C are wrong: an authorisation does not replace the taxpayer’s participation, and none of the three exceptions applies.

notes.front: What must happen to sensitive taxpayer information the site no longer needs, if it was not returned or authorised for retention?
notes.back: It must be shredded or burned.
notes.explanation: It covers anything neither handed back nor kept with the taxpayer’s authorisation.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Protecting Physical and Electronic Data”, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: Note: Any sensitive information not returned to the taxpayer or authorized by the taxpayer to be kept for retention by the site, must be shredded or burned when no longer needed.

notes.front: At closing, a volunteer finds a stack of printed acknowledgement reports with taxpayers’ names and numbers that nobody needs. What should happen to them?
notes.back: A: shred or burn them.
notes.explanation: Sensitive information not returned to taxpayers or kept with their authorisation is shredded or burned once no longer needed.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Protecting Physical and Electronic Data”, PDF p. 14
notes.evidence: Protect reports showing Submission ID Numbers and e-file Acknowledgments. Note: Any sensitive information not returned to the taxpayer or authorized by the taxpayer to be kept for retention by the site, must be shredded or burned when no longer needed.
notes.choices:
A) Shred or burn them
B) Put them in the recycling bin
C) Take them home to shred later
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: ordinary recycling does not destroy the data. C is wrong: taxpayer information must stay under the site’s control, and volunteers do not keep copies.

notes.front: What does Publication 4299 require of a strong password, and how often must volunteers change it?
notes.back: At least 8 characters, including numbers or symbols; changed periodically, at least every 90 days.
notes.explanation: Publication 4299 adds that the longer the password, the harder it is to compromise.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Minimum Security Practices for Safeguarding Taxpayer Data”, PDF p. 16
notes.evidence: Volunteer must change their passwords periodically (at a minimum, every 90 days) or as required to protect taxpayer information. Desktop software requires the use of a strong password. A strong password must: ■ Include at least 8 characters and include numbers or symbols. The longer the password, the tougher it is to compromise.

notes.front: May a site use an unprotected public wireless network to send taxpayer information?
notes.back: No, it is prohibited; any wireless network used must be encrypted and password protected.
notes.explanation: Wireless may be used only after a comprehensive risk assessment, and then only on an encrypted, password-protected network.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Use of secure wireless networks”, PDF p. 17
notes.evidence: If partners/volunteers, after conducting a comprehensive risk assessment, decide to use wireless devices to transmit taxpayer information to the tax preparation software provider, they must ensure that only an encrypted password protected wireless network is used. The use of unprotected public wireless networks is prohibited.

notes.front: What is a data breach at a volunteer site?
notes.back: When a taxpayer’s PII, physical or electronic, is shared, used or disclosed without the taxpayer’s permission.
notes.explanation: Publication 4299 divides breaches into unintentional ones (mistakes) and intentional ones.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Reporting Data Breaches”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: A VITA/TCE data breach occurs when a taxpayer’s personally identifiable information (PII) is shared, used or disclosed, whether physical or electronic, without taxpayer permission. There are two types of data breaches:

notes.front: A volunteer hands a taxpayer his return folder, which by mistake also holds a neighbour’s Form W-2. What kind of data breach is this?
notes.back: A: an unintentional data breach.
notes.explanation: Publication 4299’s unintentional type is a volunteer mistakenly providing another taxpayer’s return or documents.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Reporting Data Breaches”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: a) Unintentional (a mistake) – volunteer mistakenly provided a copy of another taxpayer’s tax return or tax documents in error. b) Intentional (on purpose) – data loss incidents such as accessing a volunteer preparer network without permission and/or theft of PII.
notes.choices:
A) An unintentional data breach
B) An intentional data breach
C) Not a breach, because it was an accident
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: intentional breaches are things like unauthorised network access or theft. C is wrong: a mistake is still a breach, of the unintentional type.

notes.front: Whom must a partner contact first when a potential data breach occurs, and when?
notes.back: The local territory office, immediately once the incident is confirmed.
notes.explanation: The territory office decides whether it meets the criteria of a potential data breach.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Reporting Data Breaches”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: When a potential data breach occurs, (unintentional or intentional) partners must contact their local SPEC Territory Office immediately upon confirmation of the incident. The territory office must review the details of the incident and determine if it meets the criteria of a potential data breach.

notes.front: A partner-owned laptop used at a site is stolen. By when must the partner tell the Internal Revenue Service?
notes.back: Immediately, and no later than the next business day after the incident is confirmed.
notes.explanation: If the laptop held taxpayer PII, the loss is also reported under the data breach guidance.
notes.source: Publication 4299 (Rev. 2-2025), Privacy, Confidentiality, and Civil Rights – A Public Trust, “Reporting Stolen and Lost Equipment”, PDF p. 19
notes.evidence: Partners must immediately notify IRS, but not later than the next business day after confirmation of the incident, if a partner owned computer is stolen or lost. If the lost or stolen equipment contained taxpayer PII data, the partner must report the loss of PII data based on data breach guidance.

notes.front: How does a deactivated return differ from a stockpiled one?
notes.back: Stockpiling holds a finished return the site could send; deactivation stops a return that cannot be finished.
notes.explanation: Deactivation follows lack of response, unresolved rejects, an unsigned Form 8879 or staffing problems, and the taxpayer is told to collect the documents.
notes.source: Publication 5166 (Rev. 10-2025), VITA/TCE Volunteer Quality Site Requirements, “E-filing Returns and Stockpiling of Returns”, PDF p. 18
notes.evidence: If due to lack of response, delays with resolving rejects, signing Form 8879 or volunteer staffing, sites must notify taxpayers that the return has been deactivated in the tax preparation software and to return to the site to pick up their tax documents.
